summary: Defines a DHCPv4 relay agent suboption that lets the relay set flags for the forwarded packet. One flag says whether the relay received the packet by unicast or broadcast, which the server can use. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A sticky note from the helper telling the server how the request first arrived.

questions: what is the dhcp relay agent flags suboption
how does a dhcp server know if a request was broadcast
what is the dhcp unicast flag
subtitle: A one-byte flag from the DHCP relay that tells the server whether the client's request arrived by unicast or broadcast.

tldr.problem: When a DHCP relay agent forwards a client's packet, the server cannot tell whether the client broadcast it or unicast it to the relay, and the server may want to treat those cases differently.
tldr.mechanism: The relay adds a Flags suboption (code 10) to the relay agent information option. Its first flag, U, is 1 for unicast and 0 for broadcast.
tldr.outcome: Servers can use the flag in their processing decisions, for example in load balancing. Relays that support it MUST include the suboption in every forwarded request.

today: RFC 5010 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2007. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why the Server Needs to Know
sections.content:
A DHCP relay agent forwards a client's DHCP packet to a server on another network. It can add extra information using the relay agent information option from RFC 3046. After a lease is granted, later DHCPREQUEST and renewal messages are normally unicast straight to the DHCP server.

Servers may change how they process a message depending on whether they got it directly by unicast, directly by broadcast, or by unicast from a relay that forwarded a client broadcast. The trouble is that some clients unicast their DHCPREQUEST or renewal packets to the relay, which forwards them on. The server then cannot tell whether the client broadcast or unicast the original.

The RFC gives an example: a server might be willing to NAK a client in the REBINDING state because its address does not match its place in the network, but not be willing to do so for a client in the RENEWING state.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mail clerk passing your letter to the boss. The boss acts differently if you shouted your request to the whole room or quietly handed it over, but the clerk never says which it was.

sections.title: The Flags Suboption Format
sections.content:
The Flags suboption is an extensible way to carry several possible flags. It has three one-octet fields: Code (the suboption code, 10), Length (1 octet) and Flags.

Only the first flag is defined so far. In the Flags octet, the high bit U is the UNICAST flag: 1 means the relay received the packet by unicast and 0 means broadcast. The remaining bits are MBZ, short for MUST BE ZERO, and are reserved for future use.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny note with a label, a size and one switch. The switch is up if the request was handed over directly and down if it was shouted to everyone.

sections.title: What the Relay Agent Does
sections.content:
A relay agent that claims to conform to this specification MUST include the suboption in every relay agent information option it adds to a forwarded DHCP request. That holds whether the packet it is forwarding arrived by broadcast or by unicast.

The reason is that the server will meet both relays that support the suboption and relays that do not. If supporting relays always include it, the server can tell a request from a non-supporting relay apart from a request from a supporting relay that received a broadcast.

A missing suboption means the relay does not support it. A present suboption with U set to 0 means the relay does support it and saw a broadcast.
sections.eli5: The helper has to attach the note every single time, even when the answer is 'shouted'. Otherwise the boss could not tell 'shouted' from 'this helper never writes notes'.

sections.title: What the DHCP Server Does
sections.content:
The server MAY use the flag to make processing decisions about the client's packet. The RFC's example is load balancing as in RFC 3074: a load-balancing server may be willing to respond to a REBINDING client, but cannot determine the client's state without this additional indication.

The suboption length is one octet. If the server receives a suboption longer than one octet, it MUST evaluate the first octet.

The RFC also warns implementors about future flags. It will not always be possible to tell relays that understand a new flag and set it to zero from relays that simply set unassigned bits to zero. So it would be a mistake to specify significant behavior changes based on zero values of flags defined in the future.
sections.eli5: The boss may use the note when deciding what to do. If the note is longer than expected, the boss reads only the first part. And nobody should assume that a blank spot on a new switch means anything.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The relay agent option depends on a trusted relationship between the relay agent and the server, as described in RFC 3046. A perimeter defense that blocks these options unless the relay is trusted can prevent fraudulent relay-agent options, but the RFC says a deeper defense using the authentication option for relay agent options (RFC 4030) SHOULD be deployed as well.

For message authentication within a domain where a shared secret can be exchanged out of band, it points to RFC 3118. Potential exposures are discussed in Section 7 of RFC 2131.

On the IANA side, suboption number 10 was assigned for the Flags suboption from the relay agent information option suboption number space.
sections.eli5: The boss has to trust the helper's notes. Blocking strangers at the door helps, and having the helper sign each note helps even more.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Relay agent flags: U (unicast = 1, broadcast = 0) then MBZ bits, reserved and must be zero.
